opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the main reason is just the trend. If you look at SWE-bench, and especially the Verified subset, progress over the past year or so has been extremely fast. When the benchmark first came out, the best systems were solving a few percent of issues. Then you got agent scaffolds, better base models, and models trained specifically to work in coding environments, and scores went from single digits to well over half the problems in a fairly short time. If you extrapolate even somewhat conservatively, you hit the ceiling around the end of 2025.

The second reason is that these tasks aren't actually that hard for something with the right skills. Most SWE-bench issues are fairly localized: there's a bug report, you find the relevant few files in the repository, make a relatively small change, and the tests pass. That's useful work, but it's not like designing a large system from scratch or coordinating a multi-month project. It's the kind of task where a competent human engineer with some familiarity with the codebase could finish in under an hour, often much less. Current models are already decent at reading code, understanding error messages, and making targeted edits. So the remaining gap is mostly about reliability and navigating the repository well, which is exactly what reinforcement learning on agentic coding tasks is improving right now.

There's also a lot of economic pressure behind it. Coding is one of the clearest commercial applications of these models, so labs have strong incentives to push on exactly this kind of capability, and SWE-bench has become the headline number people report. When a benchmark becomes a target like that, it tends to get saturated quickly.

The caveat is what "saturation" means. Some fraction of the problems are underspecified, or the tests are a bit off, so you'd never expect 100%. When I say saturated, I mean scores getting close to whatever the practical ceiling is, where further gains mostly reflect noise or quirks of the benchmark rather than real capability differences. And I'd be careful about reading too much into it when that happens. Saturating SWE-bench doesn't mean AI can replace software engineers. The hard parts of the job, like working on long-horizon projects, dealing with ambiguous requirements, and coordinating with other people, aren't really measured by it. So I expect the benchmark to fall, but I'd treat that as a much smaller milestone than the headlines will probably make it sound.

r001.rationale: The response says most issues are localized and require finding only a few relevant files and making a small change, identifying limited project context as a reason for expected saturation.

r002.rationale: It mentions the Verified subset but does not explain that its issues were human-validated or distinguish that validation from issue difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the main reason is just extrapolating the trend. If you look at how performance on SWE-bench has gone over the past year or two, it's been climbing really fast. When the benchmark first came out, models were resolving something like a few percent of the issues, and then with better scaffolding and better models that went up to maybe 20, 30, 40 percent, and now on the verified subset we're seeing numbers well above 50 percent. So if you just draw the line, you end up near the ceiling sometime around the end of 2025.

And there's a second reason, which is that the benchmark has a particular structure that makes it easier than real software engineering. The problems are self-contained, they're drawn from popular open-source Python repositories, there are unit tests that tell you unambiguously whether you've succeeded, and you don't have to deal with things like gathering requirements from a confused stakeholder or maintaining a codebase over many months. So it's exactly the kind of task that current approaches are well suited to: you can generate a lot of attempts, you can verify them against tests, and labs can do reinforcement learning on it very directly. Once a benchmark becomes a target that labs are explicitly optimizing for, it tends to saturate quickly.

I'd also add that saturation doesn't mean a hundred percent. Some fraction of the problems are mislabeled or underspecified, or the tests are flaky, so there's an effective ceiling somewhere below that. By saturation I mean models get close to that ceiling, so the benchmark stops being informative about differences between systems.

The thing I'd caution against is reading too much into this. SWE-bench saturating doesn't mean software engineers are about to be automated. It means models are good at a specific, narrow slice of what software engineers do. The gap between doing well on a benchmark like this and actually being able to replace a person on a team is still large, because so much of the job is the long-horizon, context-heavy, messy stuff that benchmarks are bad at capturing. So I'm fairly confident about the prediction, but I'd be much more cautious about what people conclude from it.

r001.rationale: It says SWE-bench problems are self-contained and do not require maintaining a codebase over many months, conveying that resolving them needs limited project context.

astra-6.text:
My expectation is mostly an extrapolation from how quickly performance has been improving. SWE-bench asks systems to resolve issues in existing codebases, and that’s a task where better models and better ways of letting them interact with a repository can both make a substantial difference. You can let the model inspect the code, run tests, see what failed, and try again. So there’s a fairly productive feedback loop, and spending more computation on a problem can improve the chance of solving it.

I also expect companies to put a lot of effort into this because software engineering is economically valuable. It’s a capability people have strong incentives to improve.

Now, by saturation I don’t necessarily mean getting literally 100 percent. Some issues may be ambiguous, or the tests may not perfectly capture whether a solution is correct. I mean reaching the point where the benchmark stops being particularly useful for distinguishing the strongest systems. That would still be quite different from automating software engineering as a whole: resolving a well-specified issue in a repository is only one part of that job.

sol-6.1.text:
The main reason is just the pace of progress. If you look at how quickly performance on SWE-bench has been improving, the end of 2025 seems like a plausible time for the benchmark to stop being very informative about differences between the best systems.

These are fairly well-specified tasks: you have a repository, an issue describing something that needs to be fixed, and a way to test whether the fix works. That makes them particularly amenable to systems that can try a solution, run tests, inspect the results, and iterate. So improvements can come both from better underlying models and from giving those models better tools and more time to work.

I wouldn't interpret saturation as meaning that software engineering is solved. Resolving an issue in an existing repository is only one part of what software engineers do. And you might stop short of literally 100 percent because some issues are ambiguous or the tests don't perfectly capture what a correct solution should be. The prediction is more that we'll need harder benchmarks to measure further progress.
